books.title: Taste This
books.art_why: Real foods and a tongue can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction We use our tongue to taste. Foods can taste salty, bitter, sour, or sweet.
pages.brief: A close-up of a person's tongue sticking out, showing the pink surface and taste buds. The tongue is the body part we use to taste foods. The background is soft and neutral, focusing entirely on the tongue to illustrate how we taste.

pages.text: Can you guess how these foods can taste?
pages.brief: A group of various foods is displayed on a simple surface. The foods are different colors and shapes, ready for someone to guess if they are salty, bitter, sour, or sweet. No people are visible, and the focus is on the foods themselves.

pages.text: Salty Taste These are pretzels. Pretzels can taste salty. We use salt to give foods a salty flavor.
pages.brief: A bowl of pretzels, golden-brown and twisted into classic shapes, sits on a table. A small pile of salt crystals is nearby, showing how salt gives foods a salty flavor. The pretzels are the main focus, clearly visible.

pages.text: Bitter Taste This is spinach. Spinach can taste bitter. Some people do not like bitter flavors.
pages.brief: A close-up of fresh spinach leaves, dark green and leafy, resting on a light-colored surface. The leaves are shown clearly to illustrate a bitter taste. No people are present, and the focus is on the spinach.

pages.text: Sour and Sweet Taste This is a lemon. Lemons can taste sour. Some people do not like sour flavors.
pages.brief: A whole lemon and a slice of lemon on a cutting board. The bright yellow citrus fruit is shown with its juicy interior. The lemon is the focus, illustrating a sour taste. The background is simple.

pages.text: This is honey. Honey can taste sweet. We use honey to give foods a sweet flavor.
pages.brief: A glass jar filled with golden honey, with a wooden dipper lifting a stream of honey. The honey is thick and shiny, illustrating a sweet flavor. The jar sits on a table with a warm light.

pages.text: These are apples. Apples can taste sweet or sour. Do you like sweet apples? Or do you like sour apples?
pages.brief: Several apples, some red and some green, arranged on a table. One apple is cut in half to show the inside. The apples are fresh and colorful, shown to illustrate that they can taste sweet or sour.

pages.text: Conclusion How do your favorite foods taste?
pages.brief: A close-up of a plate with several different foods, each with distinct colors and textures. The foods are arranged to represent different tastes. The scene invites the viewer to consider how their favorite foods taste.

books.title: Firefighters
books.art_why: Firefighters and their trucks are real people and machines at work today, so real photographs exist.

pages.text: Have you ever heard a fire truck racing to a fire? The truck is full of firefighters. Firefighters help keep us safe.
pages.brief: A red fire truck races along a city street with its lights flashing, firefighters in helmets and dark turnout gear seated inside the cab. The truck is full of firefighters on their way to a fire, with buildings lining the street behind them.

pages.text: Firefighters fight many kinds of fires.
pages.brief: Firefighters in helmets and heavy gear fight different kinds of fires: one sprays water at flames leaping from a burning house, while another beats at a line of fire spreading across dry grass in an open field.

pages.text: Firefighters use many tools. Firefighters use ladders to reach high places. Firefighters help keep us safe.
pages.brief: A firefighter climbs a tall ladder propped against a high building, reaching up toward a window far above the ground. Below, another firefighter in gear holds the base of the ladder steady on the pavement.

pages.text: Firefighters use hoses to spray water. Firefighters help keep us safe.
pages.brief: Two firefighters grip a thick hose together and spray a powerful stream of water into flames. Water arcs through the air while their boots stay planted on the ground, hoses coiled beside them.

pages.text: Firefighters use axes to break down doors. They use masks to breathe safely.
pages.brief: A firefighter swings a heavy axe at a closed door, splintering the wood. Beside them, another firefighter wears a face mask with an air tank, breathing safely through the smoke that fills the doorway.

pages.text: Firefighters use machines. They use trucks and boats to spray water on fires. They use planes and helicopters to dump water on forest fires.
pages.brief: Firefighting machines at work: a fire truck and a fire boat spray water, while a plane and a helicopter fly low over a forest, dumping water onto the burning trees below.

pages.text: Firefighters are strong. They help keep us safe.
pages.brief: A strong firefighter in full gear lifts and carries heavy equipment, muscles straining, boots firm on the ground. Others stand nearby with hoses and tools, ready to move and help keep people safe.

pages.text: Firefighters go to school. They learn to fight fires. They learn to keep people safe.
pages.brief: Firefighters train at a school, standing in a line in their gear while an instructor shows them how to fight fires. Trainees practice with hoses and ladders, learning how to keep people safe.

pages.text: Firefighters help keep fires from starting. They teach other people about fires, too.
pages.brief: A firefighter talks to a group of people, showing them how to stop fires from starting. The listeners sit and stand attentively as the firefighter points to safety equipment and explains fire dangers.

pages.text: Firefighters help people and save lives. Firefighters help keep us safe.
pages.brief: A firefighter in helmet and gear leads a frightened person by the arm out of danger, guiding them to safety. Others help nearby, carrying people away from harm and saving lives.

books.title: Smart Crows
books.art_why: Crows are real animals that exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Crows are smart. They are as smart as elephants. They are as smart as apes.
pages.brief: A glossy black crow perches on a park fence, head tilted and eye bright. In the background, an elephant walks across a grassy savanna and an ape sits among leafy branches, showing the crow beside other smart animals.

pages.text: Crows solve problems. Crows use tools.
pages.brief: A crow stands on the ground holding a small tool in its beak, focused on a problem in front of it with careful attention. Another crow watches nearby, showing crows solving problems and using tools.

pages.text: Crows build nests from things we throw away.
pages.brief: A crow carries a bright bottle cap and a scrap of paper to a messy nest in a tree. The nest is woven from discarded string, plastic bits, and twigs, with the crow adding another found item to build it.

pages.text: Crows let cars crack nuts for them. Crows drop nuts on the road. Cars drive over the nuts. When the light turns red, crows hop out and fetch their snack!
pages.brief: A crow drops a nut onto a busy road as a car drives over it. The car’s tire cracks the shell. At a red traffic light, the crow hops onto the road and fetches the broken nut, then lifts it in its beak.

pages.text: Hey, it’s Joe! So it is. Hey Joe, what do you know? Crows learn human faces. They can pick out those faces in a crowd.
pages.brief: A crow stands on a city sidewalk and looks directly at a human face in a busy crowd. Around the person, many other faces blur past, while the crow’s dark eye stays fixed on the one it recognizes.

pages.text: Use your please. Crows use soft calls with family members. Crows use louder calls with other crows.
pages.brief: Two crows sit close together on a branch, one giving a soft, gentle call to the other. Nearby, a third crow stands farther away and opens its beak in a louder call, showing crows using soft family calls and louder calls with other crows.

pages.text: Crows work together to find food. They work together to protect their family.
pages.brief: Two crows work side by side on the ground, one pulling at a food scrap while the other keeps watch. Behind them, a third crow rests near a nest in a tree, showing crows working together to find food and protect their family.

pages.text: Do I Nope. know you? I’m just here to help. Crows even defend crows they don’t know.
pages.brief: A crow stands between an unfamiliar crow and a nest, wings slightly spread to shield the other bird. The unfamiliar crow looks cautious but stays close, showing crows defending even a crow they do not know.

pages.text: Crows gather to say good-bye to dead crows.
pages.brief: Several crows gather quietly on the grass around a dead crow lying on the ground. They stand close together with heads lowered, forming a loose circle in a still, somber scene that shows crows gathering to say good-bye.

pages.text: Crows watch and learn and feel, like us. Crows are smart, like you.
pages.brief: A crow perches on a low branch, watching a child nearby with calm, alert eyes. The child looks back at the crow, showing that crows watch and learn and feel, like us, and are smart, like you.

books.title: Night Animals
books.art_why: Real night animals and their habitats can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Some animals are active at night, when it is dark. These animals sleep during the day while the Sun shines.
pages.brief: A dark nighttime landscape shows several animals awake and active, moving about while the sky is black. In a bright daytime scene, the same animals lie resting and asleep on the ground as the Sun shines overhead.

pages.text: These animals have special eyes to help them see in the dark. Most of them also hear and smell well. Their senses help them find food at night.
pages.brief: A close view of a nighttime animal shows large, shining eyes looking through darkness, with ears alert and nose close to the ground. The animal searches for food in the dark, using its eyes, hearing and smell to find something to eat.

pages.text: In the Air This owl is active at night. It catches mice and rats in the dark.
pages.brief: An owl flies through the dark night air with wings spread wide, hunting. Below, a mouse and a rat run on the ground. The owl looks down and catches the small animals in its talons in the darkness.

pages.text: This bat is active at night. It eats fruit and nectar in the dark.
pages.brief: A bat is active at night, flying through the dark air with wings spread and holding a piece of fruit. It sips nectar from a flower and eats the fruit in the darkness, feeding at night.

pages.text: In Water This nurse shark is active at night. It finds crabs and clams in the dark.
pages.brief: A nurse shark is active at night, swimming through dark water near the seafloor. Crabs and clams rest on the sandy bottom. The shark moves toward them, finding crabs and clams in the dark water.

pages.text: This hermit crab is active at night. It looks for little fish and worms in the dark.
pages.brief: A hermit crab is active at night, moving through dark water near the bottom. Little fish swim nearby and worms move in the dark. The hermit crab searches for little fish and worms in the darkness, looking for food.

pages.text: On Land This tiger is active at night. It hunts deer and wild pigs in the dark.
pages.brief: A tiger is active at night, moving through dark land with its eyes fixed ahead. Deer and wild pigs stand nearby in the darkness. The tiger hunts, moving toward the deer and wild pigs in the dark.

pages.text: Are you active at night or during the day?
pages.brief: A child is shown awake in the dark at night, then active in bright daylight. The child stands under a black night sky and later under a sunny day sky, showing activity at night and during the day.

books.title: Are You From India?
books.art_why: All the animals are real and alive today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: I am from a country called India. Many animals live here.
pages.brief: A wide view of an Indian landscape with dry grass, scattered green trees and a warm sky. Several wild animals stand among the bushes: a peacock, a monkey, a tiger and an elephant. In the foreground a young child in simple clothes smiles with arms open toward the animals.

pages.text: I am from India. I wave my beautiful green tail.
pages.brief: A peacock stands on short green grass in bright sunlight, its huge tail feathers fanned out behind it in a shimmering green fan. The bird's blue head and neck are held high as it turns slightly, showing the full spread of its tail.

pages.text: I am from India. You may spot my dark face as I leap from tree to tree.
pages.brief: A lion-tailed macaque with a dark face and a fringe of black hair around its head grips a branch high in a forest tree. Its long tail hangs down as it leaps, body stretched, from one tree to the next in the green canopy.

pages.text: I am from India. I have a wide head that looks like a hood.
pages.brief: An Indian cobra rests on dry, dusty ground beside low grass. Its head and neck are lifted and spread wide into a flat hood, showing the pale mark on the back of the hood, while the long body coils behind it in the sun.

pages.text: I am from India. I am as big as a house, and I love to play in water.
pages.brief: A large Asian elephant stands knee-deep in a wide river, water splashing around its legs. It curls its trunk and sprays water over its own back, ears fanned out, with green banks and trees behind it under a bright sky.

pages.text: I am from India. I have orange and black stripes, and I move silently through the forest.
pages.brief: A Bengal tiger with orange fur and black stripes walks quietly through thick forest, tall grass and leafy branches around it. Its head is low, eyes forward, one heavy paw lifting as it moves silently between the trees in dappled light.

pages.text: I am from India. My long, thin snout has a bump on the end.
pages.brief: A gharial lies on a sandy riverbank beside slow green water, its long, thin snout stretched forward and the odd rounded bump raised at the tip of its snout. Its short legs rest on the sand and its eyes watch ahead.

pages.text: I am from India. I am small but brave and famous for hunting snakes.
pages.brief: A small grey mongoose stands alert on rocky ground, its body low and slender, tail raised, whiskers forward and dark eyes bright. It looks ready to spring, small but bold, with dry grass and stones around it.

pages.text: I am from India. My thick, shaggy coat protects me in the cold mountains.
pages.brief: A yak with a thick, shaggy brown coat stands on a cold mountain slope, its long hair hanging almost to the ground. Behind it rise rocky Himalayan peaks with patches of snow and a pale, chilly sky.

pages.text: All of these animals are from India, and I am from India, too.
pages.brief: The child from the first page stands on grassy ground with the animals gathered around: the peacock, the macaque, the cobra, the elephant, the tiger, the gharial, the mongoose and the yak. The child smiles in the middle of the group under a warm sky.

books.title: Some Birds Go
books.art_why: Real birds and migration are shown in nature.

pages.text: Up in the sky, birds fly by. Where are the birds going?
pages.brief: A group of birds flies high across the open sky, wings spread, moving together in one direction. They are seen from below as they pass by, with only sky around them and no landing place in view.

pages.text: N Some birds migrate to other places for part of the year. Many migrate before winter in order to survive.
pages.brief: Several birds travel together across a wide outdoor space, flying on their way to another place as the season turns colder. The group moves steadily, showing part of a yearly journey made to survive winter.

pages.text: This bird migrates for fruit in winter. It returns for worms and insects in spring.
pages.brief: One bird sits beside fruiting branches in a cold winter scene, feeding on fruit. Later, on thawing spring ground, the same bird stands near worms and insects that have appeared for it to eat. A clear change of season is shown.

pages.text: This bird migrates in a V-shaped flock.
pages.brief: A flock of birds flies across the sky in a clear V shape, with one bird at the front and others lined up behind on both sides. Their wings are spread as they travel together through open air.

pages.text: This bird migrates at night and rests during the day.
pages.brief: A single bird flies through the dark night sky, wings beating as it travels. In daylight, the same bird rests on a branch, settled and still, after its nighttime journey. The two times of day are shown side by side.

pages.text: This bird migrates when the air grows too cold.
pages.brief: A bird takes flight over an open landscape as cold air fills the scene. Its wings are spread wide, and it moves away through the chilly sky, leaving the cooling place behind. The air looks brisk and wintry.

pages.text: This bird often migrates alone.
pages.brief: One bird flies alone through a wide, empty sky, with no other birds nearby. Its wings are spread as it travels by itself, a single small shape moving across the open air. The lone bird is the only subject in view.

pages.text: This bird migrates in a flock of thousands.
pages.brief: A huge flock of birds fills the sky, thousands of wings moving together in a dense crowd. The birds stretch across the open air, flying as one enormous group with no single leader visible. The flock covers a vast space.

pages.text: This bird migrates across the water without stopping.
pages.brief: A bird flies low over open water, wings spread and steady, crossing without landing. No shore or resting place is visible, only the wide stretch of water beneath and around it. The bird keeps moving over the endless surface.

pages.text: Some birds fly down a mountain to migrate. Some birds fly thousands of miles to migrate. Wherever these birds go, they’ll always come back.
pages.brief: Some birds glide down from a mountain slope, while others travel in a long line across a vast landscape. The scene shows birds flying far across the land and then returning, as if their journey will always bring them back.

books.title: Sleds
books.art_why: Sleds, snowy hills and dog teams are real things that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Who Sleds? Sometimes snow makes travel tricky. Sometimes people use sleds to travel on snow.
pages.brief: A snowy village path with deep, soft snow across it, and a person steering a small wooden sled loaded with a bundle along the snow, leaving a fresh track behind in the white ground.

pages.text: Some people use sleds for fun. Some people use sleds for sports. Some people use sleds for work.
pages.brief: A wide snowy scene split three ways: children sliding down a gentle hill laughing on a bright plastic sled, a racer crouched low on a sports sled, and a worker hauling a loaded wooden sled across flat snow.

pages.text: Fun Sleds This sled is long and wooden. It glides quickly on the snow.
pages.brief: A long wooden sled with wide slatted boards and curved front tips sits on a slope of packed white snow, its runners cutting forward, pine trees and soft falling snow behind it on a bright winter day.

pages.text: This sled is filled with air. Spinning down a hill is fun.
pages.brief: A round inflatable sled filled with air, shiny and puffy, spins down a snowy hill, throwing up a spray of white snow, with more children waiting at the top of the slope behind.

pages.text: Sport Sleds This sled holds four people. Riders steer around sharp bends.
pages.brief: A four-person bobsled with four riders in helmets races through a sharp bend on a snow-walled track, the team leaning together as the sled tilts around the curve.

pages.text: This sled zips down an icy track. The rider goes head first.
pages.brief: A single rider in a tight suit and helmet lies head first on a low sled, speeding down a shining icy track with high curved walls, frozen spray around the runners.

pages.text: Work Sleds This sled helps carry things. Dog teams sometimes race over the snow.
pages.brief: A loaded wooden sled carries boxes and bundles over flat snow while a team of dogs in harness runs ahead, pulling it across a wide white open landscape.

pages.text: This sled has a rope. You can pull people or things on top.
pages.brief: A simple flat sled with a thick rope tied to its front rests on snowy ground, a person pulling the rope while a child sits on top, snow all around them.

pages.text: Many Sleds Sleds and snow just go together. They help make winter fun.
pages.brief: A snowy hill crowded with many kinds of sleds, long wooden ones, an air sled, a rope sled and a racing sled, with families and children enjoying a bright winter day outdoors.

books.title: Animal Dads
books.art_why: Real animal fathers and their young exist today, so photographs fit best.

pages.text: Some animal dads don’t help much. These dads don’t help at all!
pages.brief: An animal dad lies apart from a group of young animals, not helping them. The young animals are nearby, and the dad stays where he is, showing a father that does not help at all.

pages.text: Other animal dads are great! Which animal dads are those?
pages.brief: Several different animal dads are shown with their young in a natural setting, each one close and attentive. They stand or sit beside their babies, looking after them, while the question asks which animal dads are great.

pages.text: This dad guards and cares for his chicks. He helps them all by himself for almost two years.
pages.brief: A bird dad stands guard over his chicks, keeping them close and safe. He cares for them all by himself, with no other helper nearby, and he stays with them through almost two years of growing.

pages.text: This dad cleans bugs from his babies’ fur. He helps feed them. He carries them, too.
pages.brief: A furry animal dad gently cleans bugs from his babies’ fur. He helps feed them and carries them with him, holding them close as he moves. His babies stay near him while he keeps them clean and cared for.

pages.text: This dad holds eggs in his mouth. He helps them stay safe until they are born.
pages.brief: An animal dad holds several eggs in his open mouth, keeping them safe. He stays still and careful so the eggs are protected until the babies are born, with the eggs clearly held inside his mouth.

pages.text: This dad eats food and spits it back up. Then he feeds it to his pups. Yum! He helps his pups grow strong.
pages.brief: An animal dad eats food and then spits it back up, feeding the soft food to his pups. The pups gather close to him, and he helps them grow strong by giving them the food he brings back.

pages.text: This dad carries tadpoles on his back. He helps them reach water.
pages.brief: An animal dad carries many tadpoles on his back, moving carefully toward water. The tadpoles cling to him as he travels, and he keeps them safe on the way. He helps them reach the water they need to grow.

pages.text: This dad holds an egg on his feet. He helps keep it warm in the cold.
pages.brief: A bird dad stands in the cold with a single egg resting on his feet. He holds the egg carefully and keeps it warm, protecting it from the cold ground while he waits for it to hatch.

pages.text: This dad holds thousands of eggs in his pouch. He helps them grow and hatch.
pages.brief: An animal dad has a pouch filled with thousands of tiny eggs. He carries the eggs in his pouch, keeping them close, and he helps them grow and hatch inside the safe pouch. The eggs stay protected there.

pages.text: These dads help out with their young, too!
pages.brief: Several animal dads are shown with their young, staying close and helping them. Each dad is near his babies, looking after them in his own way, showing that these fathers help out with their young too.

books.title: Hibernation
books.art_why: Real animals and real winter scenes can be photographed.

pages.text: No Food in Winter Some animals can’t find food in the winter. Some of these animals hibernate.
pages.brief: A snowy winter woodland clearing with bare trees and deep snow. A red fox stands still, sniffing the cold air, while a squirrel sits on a low branch. No food is visible on the frozen ground.

pages.text: What Is Hibernating? Hibernating is like a deep sleep. This sleep can last for weeks.
pages.brief: Inside a dark earthen den, a small brown bat hangs upside down wrapped in its wings, eyes closed in deep sleep. Dried leaves and soft soil line the hollow space around it.

pages.text: Animals breathe slowly when they hibernate. Their hearts beat slower. They do not eat.
pages.brief: A hibernating brown bear curled in a nest of dry leaves inside a cave. Its chest barely rises, and its eyes are shut. Beside it, a tiny mouse also sleeps, very still.

pages.text: How Do They Stay Alive? Hibernating animals eat lots of food before winter. The food stays in their bodies as fat.
pages.brief: A late-autumn forest with fallen leaves. A black bear eats berries from a bush, a squirrel nibbles nuts on a log, and a bat catches insects in the dim air. Their bodies store the food as fat.

pages.text: Animals live off this fat while they sleep. They also need a safe place to sleep.
pages.brief: A sleeping squirrel curled in a hollow tree trunk, its body round and still. Soft dry grass and bark line the safe hollow. Outside the opening, snow falls steadily past the tree.

pages.text: They need to be safe from the cold. They need to be safe from hungry animals.
pages.brief: A hibernating turtle buried in soft mud at the bottom of a pond, safe beneath the cold water. Above the icy surface, a hungry fox peers down but cannot reach it.

pages.text: Hibernating Animals Some snakes and frogs hibernate. Some turtles and mice hibernate. Some squirrels and bats hibernate.
pages.brief: A rocky woodland floor in winter with several hibernating animals: a snake coiled under a log, a frog buried in mud, a turtle in its shell, a mouse in a burrow, a squirrel in a tree hollow, and a bat hanging from a branch.

pages.text: Some bears hibernate. Some raccoons and skunks hibernate, too. All the hibernating animals wake up in the spring.
pages.brief: A bear, a raccoon and a skunk emerge from dens and hollows into a sunny spring forest with new green shoots. The bear stretches, the raccoon blinks, and the skunk steps out. Snow melts around them.

books.title: At the Airport
books.art_why: Real modern airport scenes with travelers, buses and planes are best shown with photographs.

pages.text: What happens at the airport?
pages.brief: An airport building stands open with travelers walking toward the entrance, showing the busy place where many people come and go. The scene introduces the airport and the people who travel through it on their journeys.

pages.text: Travelers park their cars in big parking lots at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers park their cars in a big parking lot at the airport. Several cars sit in marked spaces, and travelers step out of their vehicles, ready to continue their trip into the airport building. The lot is wide and open.

pages.text: Travelers take buses to go to the main building at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers take a bus to go to the main building at the airport. The bus carries them from the parking area, and travelers stand or sit with their belongings as they ride toward the large main building.

pages.text: Travelers stand in line to check in with their airline at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers stand in line to check in with their airline at the airport. The line stretches toward the check-in desk, and travelers wait their turn, facing the counter with their belongings as they prepare to continue through the airport.

pages.text: Travelers hand over their large bags at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers hand over their large bags at the airport counter. The big bags are passed across the desk, and the travelers stand together, ready for the next step of their trip through the airport before their flight.

pages.text: Travelers are searched to keep everyone safe at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers are searched at an airport checkpoint to keep everyone safe. They stand still as the safety check is done, and the search helps keep everyone safe before travelers continue into the airport for their trip.

pages.text: Travelers ride on moving sidewalks to get around faster at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers ride on a moving sidewalk inside the airport. They stand on the flat moving path as it carries them forward, and the moving sidewalk helps them get around the airport faster during their journey.

pages.text: Travelers buy food and magazines before their flights at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers buy food and magazines at the airport before their flights. They stop at a shop counter inside the building, with snacks and magazines, choosing items to take with them as they wait for their flight.

pages.text: Travelers wait to get on their planes at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers wait to get on their planes at the airport. They stand or sit with their belongings in a seating area, looking toward the planes as they wait for their turn to get on the plane.

pages.text: Travelers get on their planes and fly away at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers get on their planes at the airport and fly away. Some walk up the steps into the plane, and the plane lifts into the sky, carrying the travelers away from the airport on their trip.

books.title: Tunnels
books.art_why: Tunnels are real places people use today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Tunnels are long, narrow, covered passages. People use many kinds of tunnels.
pages.brief: A long, narrow, covered tunnel passage stretches ahead, and people walk through it. The view shows the tunnel as a passage with a roof and sides, making clear what a tunnel looks like and how people use it.

pages.text: Some tunnels go underground. They help people avoid traffic.
pages.brief: An underground tunnel runs beneath a busy road, and people travel through it in cars. Above the tunnel, traffic is visible on the road, while the tunnel gives people a way to avoid the traffic by going underground.

pages.text: Some tunnels go underwater. They help people avoid taking boats.
pages.brief: An underwater tunnel crosses beneath the water, and people travel through it instead of taking a boat. The tunnel is shown passing under the water’s surface, giving people a dry route from one side to the other.

pages.text: Some tunnels go through mountains. They help people avoid going around or over mountains.
pages.brief: A tunnel cuts through a mountain, and people travel through it to reach the other side. The mountain rises above the tunnel, showing that the passage helps people avoid going around the mountain or climbing over it.

pages.text: Some tunnels go under roads. They help people walk and bike safely.
pages.brief: A tunnel passes under a road, and people walk and bike through it. Above the tunnel is the road, while the tunnel gives pedestrians and cyclists a safe way to cross beneath the busy traffic.

pages.text: Some tunnels go deep into the Earth. They help people get rocks and metals.
pages.brief: A deep tunnel goes down into the Earth, where people work to get rocks and metals. The tunnel opening and passage show how people travel deep underground to reach the rocks and metals hidden there.

pages.text: Some tunnels have pipes. They help people get water.
pages.brief: A tunnel contains pipes running along its inside, and people use it to carry water. The pipes are shown inside the tunnel passage, making clear how the tunnel helps people get water from one place to another.

pages.text: Some tunnels are slides. They help people have fun.
pages.brief: A tunnel is shaped like a slide, and people slide through it for fun. The slide tunnel curves and drops, showing people enjoying a playful ride through a tunnel made for amusement rather than travel.

pages.text: Some tunnels are hidden. They help people travel in secret.
pages.brief: A hidden tunnel is shown in a secret place, and people travel through it quietly. The tunnel is partly concealed, showing how it lets people move from place to place without being easily seen by others.

pages.text: Tunnels help people and things move from place to place.
pages.brief: People and things move from place to place through tunnels. The scene shows different tunnels in use, with people traveling and things being carried, making clear how tunnels help movement from one place to another.

books.title: The Food Chain
books.art_why: Real plants and animals can be photographed.

pages.text: All plants need food in order to live. Green plants make food. They need air, water, and sunlight to make food. Most plants need soil, too.
pages.brief: Green plants grow in soil outdoors with their leaves spread toward bright sunlight. Water droplets sit on the leaves and soil, and air moves around the plants, showing the green plants living and making food.

pages.text: They are called plant eaters. These animals eat plants. All animals need food in order to live.
pages.brief: Several plant-eating animals stand in a natural grassy field, each eating green plants. The animals are shown feeding on leaves and stems, with green plants around them, making clear that animals need food to live.

pages.text: These animals eat other animals. They are called meat eaters.
pages.brief: A meat-eating animal in a natural setting stands over another animal and eats it. The animal is shown feeding on its catch, with the surrounding ground and plants making clear that some animals eat other animals.

pages.text: Let’s look at a food chain. The plants make food, which animals eat. Most food chains begin with plants. are part of a food chain. Plant eaters and meat eaters.
pages.brief: A natural scene shows green plants growing, a plant-eating animal eating leaves, and a meat-eating animal nearby. The plants and the two kinds of eaters are linked in a food chain, showing how most food chains begin with plants.

pages.text: A grasshopper eats the leaves of a plant. The grasshopper grows bigger. A frog eats the grasshopper. The frog grows bigger.
pages.brief: On a green plant, a grasshopper chews a leaf and grows bigger. Nearby, a frog catches and eats the grasshopper, and the frog grows bigger. Both animals are shown in a garden or meadow among green leaves.

pages.text: The fish grows bigger. A fish eats the frog.
pages.brief: Underwater in a pond or river, a fish catches a frog and eats it. The fish grows bigger as it feeds, and the frog is held in the fish’s mouth while the surrounding water shows the natural setting.

pages.text: A small bear catches the fish. The bear eats the fish. The bear grows bigger.
pages.brief: At the edge of water, a small bear catches a fish, eats the fish, and grows bigger. The bear is shown in a natural setting with the fish in its paws or mouth, feeding on it.

pages.text: What are the other parts? The grasshopper is the second part. The green plant is the first part. This food chain has five parts.
pages.brief: A natural scene shows the five living parts of the food chain together: a green plant, a grasshopper, a frog, a fish, and a small bear, arranged in a meadow and water setting to show the complete chain.

books.title: Seashells
books.art_why: Seashells and mollusks exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Some animals grow bones inside their body. These bones are called a skeleton.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of an animal shown against a plain background, its bones visible inside the body as a skeleton. The skeleton runs along the back and through the legs, with the animal's soft outline around it. No outer shell is shown.

pages.text: Some animals grow bones outside their body. These bones are called shells.
pages.brief: An animal shown from the side against a plain background, with a hard, bone-like shell covering the outside of its body. The shell sits over the back and sides, and the soft animal is tucked underneath it.

pages.text: Some animals that live in the ocean grow seashells. These animals are called mollusks.
pages.brief: Several mollusks on the sandy ocean floor, each with a soft body inside a seashell. One shell is curled, one is cone-shaped, and one is round. Clear blue water surrounds them, and the shells rest on the sand.

pages.text: Mollusks are soft, but their seashells are hard, like bones. Seashells protect mollusks from other animals. Seashells are also homes for mollusks.
pages.brief: A mollusk with a soft body tucked deep inside a hard shell on the ocean floor. The shell is closed tight, and a small fish swims nearby. The hard shell covers the soft animal completely, with only a tiny gap at the edge.

pages.text: This mollusk lives in a seashell. Its seashell is bumpy.
pages.brief: A mollusk inside a bumpy seashell on the ocean floor. The shell's surface is covered in raised lumps and ridges, and the soft animal shows at the shell's opening. Sand and blue water surround the shell.

pages.text: This mollusk lives in a seashell. Its seashell is striped.
pages.brief: A mollusk inside a striped seashell resting on the ocean floor. Dark bands run around the shell in clear stripes, and the soft body peeks out at the opening. Small grains of sand and blue water are around it.

pages.text: This mollusk lives in a seashell. Its seashell is spotted.
pages.brief: A mollusk inside a spotted seashell on the ocean floor. Round spots dot the shell's surface, and the soft animal is visible at the shell's opening. The shell sits on sand with blue water around it.

pages.text: This mollusk lives in a seashell. Its seashell is very large.
pages.brief: A very large seashell on the ocean floor with a mollusk inside. The shell is much bigger than the other shells around it, and its opening is wide. The soft body shows at the edge, and blue water surrounds the scene.

pages.text: When mollusks die, they leave their shells behind.
pages.brief: Empty seashells lying on the ocean floor, with no mollusks inside. Some shells are curled, some are cone-shaped, and some are round. They rest on the sand in clear blue water, left behind after the mollusks died.

pages.text: Now other animals may live in seashells that mollusks have left behind.
pages.brief: A small sea animal living inside an empty seashell on the ocean floor. The animal's body fills the shell's opening, and other empty shells lie nearby on the sand. Blue water surrounds them.

books.title: Are You From Brazil?
books.art_why: Real Brazilian animals and habitats can be photographed.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. Many animals live here, too.
pages.brief: A wide view of a Brazilian forest and riverbank, with several different wild animals visible among trees and near the water. The animals are at home in this habitat, some standing, some perched, and some moving through the greenery.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. I look like a red fox with long legs. A hairy mane rises along my back.
pages.brief: A maned wolf stands in open Brazilian grassland. It has long legs and a reddish-brown body like a red fox, with a dark hairy mane rising along its back. It looks across the grass, alert and still.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. My long tongue grabs insects to eat.
pages.brief: A giant anteater stands near a patch of ground with insects in a Brazilian grassy area. It stretches out its very long tongue to catch insects, reaching toward them. Its shaggy coat and long snout are clearly visible.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. I am the largest rodent in the world.
pages.brief: A large capybara stands beside a quiet Brazilian river or wetland. It is the biggest rodent shown, with a sturdy body, short legs and coarse brown fur. Grasses and water plants grow around it in the warm habitat.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. My skin is many pretty colors, but don’t touch me. I can kill with my poison.
pages.brief: A brightly colored poison dart frog sits on a wet green leaf in a Brazilian rainforest. Its skin shows many pretty colors, and it looks small but dangerous in the damp shade. Rainforest plants surround it.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. I am a small monkey with a long tail.
pages.brief: A small monkey with a long tail clings to a tree branch in a Brazilian forest. Its tail hangs down behind it as it looks around the leaves. The monkey is tiny compared with the branches and trunks around it.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. I am the heaviest snake in the world.
pages.brief: A huge green anaconda lies partly in a Brazilian river, its thick body coiled in the water. It is the heaviest snake shown, resting among river plants. The water and muddy bank surround its large form.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. I am very colorful with my long bill. Some people keep me as a pet.
pages.brief: A colorful toucan perches on a branch in a Brazilian tree. It has a very long bill and bright feathers, and it faces forward among green leaves. The bird sits calmly in the warm forest.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. Watch out if you swim in the river. My teeth are sharp!
pages.brief: A piranha swims in a Brazilian river, its sharp teeth visible in its open mouth. The fish is shown close to the dark water surface, with river plants nearby. Its body is sleek and its eye watches the water around it.

pages.text: All these animals are from Brazil. I am from Brazil, too!
pages.brief: A Brazilian child stands outdoors in a sunny natural setting, smiling beside a group of the animals from the book. The animals are gathered around in a lively scene, and the child points to them with pride. Brazil's plants and warm light fill the background.

books.title: At the Watering Hole
books.art_why: Real savanna animals at a watering hole can be photographed.

pages.text: It is the dry season on the African savanna. Animals come to the watering hole to drink.
pages.brief: On the dry African savanna, several wild animals gather around a watering hole. The ground is dry and dusty. The animals stand near the water, coming to drink during the dry season. The scene shows the watering hole as a meeting place for wildlife.

pages.text: Some animals come alone to drink. A small bird bows to take a drink.
pages.brief: At the watering hole, a small bird stands alone at the edge of the water. It bows its head down toward the surface to take a drink. The savanna is dry around it. No other animals are close by as the bird drinks alone.

pages.text: A tall giraffe bends to take a drink.
pages.brief: A tall giraffe stands at the watering hole on the dry savanna. It bends its long neck down low toward the water to take a drink. The giraffe comes alone, with open dry ground around the water and no other animals crowding it.

pages.text: A big hippo dives to take a drink.
pages.brief: A big hippo is at the watering hole. It dives down into the water to take a drink. The hippo is alone at the water’s edge on the dry African savanna, with the watering hole stretching around it and dry ground nearby.

pages.text: A heavy rhino stops to take a drink.
pages.brief: A heavy rhino stands at the watering hole on the dry savanna. It stops at the water’s edge to take a drink. The rhino is alone, with its large body close to the water and dry ground around the hole.

pages.text: Some animals come together to drink. A flock of storks comes to take a drink.
pages.brief: At the watering hole, a flock of storks gathers together to drink. The birds stand close as a group at the water’s edge on the dry African savanna. They come together, with many storks sharing the same place by the water.

pages.text: A parade of elephants comes to take a drink.
pages.brief: A parade of elephants comes to the watering hole to drink. The elephants move together in a line near the water on the dry African savanna. They gather as a group at the edge, sharing the watering hole with one another.

pages.text: A pack of dogs comes to take a drink.
pages.brief: A pack of dogs comes together to the watering hole to drink. The dogs stand as a group near the water on the dry savanna. They gather at the edge, with several dogs close to one another by the watering hole.

pages.text: A herd of zebras comes to take a drink.
pages.brief: A herd of zebras comes to the watering hole to drink. The zebras stand together in a group at the water’s edge on the dry African savanna. Many zebras share the watering hole, gathering close as they come to drink.

pages.text: Some animals come to drink and hunt. Lions, leopards, and hyenas look for a meal.
pages.brief: At the watering hole, lions, leopards, and hyenas come to drink and hunt. They look for a meal near the water on the dry African savanna. These animals are shown together at the watering hole, searching for food.

books.title: Hatching Eggs
books.art_why: Real chicks, eggs, sinks and classroom incubators exist today, so photographs are possible.

pages.text: Chicks are baby chickens. Chicks hatch from eggs.
pages.brief: A fluffy yellow chick stands on soft straw beside a cracked white eggshell, with two whole eggs resting nearby in a warm nest. The chick's tiny wings are spread slightly and its beak is open. Soft, warm light falls across the straw and the eggs.

pages.text: You can hatch chicks at school.
pages.brief: A bright classroom with wooden tables and tall windows. Four children sit together at one table, leaning in to look at a small row of white eggs resting in a carton, while a teacher stands behind them, smiling and pointing gently toward the eggs.

pages.text: First, wash your hands. This helps you and the eggs stay clean.
pages.brief: A young child stands at a classroom sink, sleeves pushed up, rubbing soapy hands together under running water. Bubbles sit on the child's fingers and wrists, and a bar of soap rests on the edge of the sink. Tiled wall behind, warm bright light.

pages.text: Next, mark the eggs with an X and an O. This helps you tell one side from the other.
pages.brief: Two hands hold a single white egg over a table. A pencil tip touches the shell, drawing a neat X. Beside the hands, three more eggs lie in a carton, one marked with an X and one with an O. A child's face peers down, concentrating.

pages.text: Then, put the eggs inside an incubator. This helps the eggs stay warm.
pages.brief: A clear plastic incubator sits on a classroom table, its lid open. A child's hands carefully lower a white egg inside, setting it beside the other eggs already resting on the incubator floor. The child's face is calm and focused, classroom shelves blurred behind.

pages.text: Next, put water inside the incubator. This keeps the eggs from getting dry.
pages.brief: Close view of the incubator on the table. A child pours water from a small cup into a shallow channel inside the incubator, while eggs sit in their places nearby. Droplets cling to the plastic. The child's hand steadies the cup, careful and slow.

pages.text: Each day, turn the eggs three times. This helps the growing chicks move around.
pages.brief: A child's hand gently rolls one egg over in the incubator, turning it from its X side toward its O side. Two other eggs wait nearby, warm under the light. The classroom window and a low shelf of books show softly behind.

pages.text: In about three weeks, check the eggs for cracks. Finally, the chicks will hatch over the next day or two!
pages.brief: A child leans close to the incubator, eyes wide, studying a fine crack running across one eggshell. Beside it, a chick has pushed free of its shell, damp and small, legs wobbly. Other eggs still lie whole, warm light over everything.

pages.text: Wait one more day before you touch the chicks. Then, feed the chicks.
pages.brief: Inside a shallow box lined with soft bedding, three fluffy chicks stand together. A child's hand rests at the edge of the box, not touching them, while a small dish of chick food sits nearby. The chicks stretch their necks toward the dish.

pages.text: Last, find them a good home.
pages.brief: A child carries a small box of chirping chicks across a sunny farmyard, toward a wooden coop with straw inside. A smiling adult holds the coop door open. Green grass, a low fence and blue sky stretch behind them.

books.title: Cascarones
books.art_why: Cascarones are real painted eggshells made and used today, so a photo fits.

pages.text: Cascarones are painted eggshells. Cascarones help people celebrate in Mexico and the United States. Word Wise.
pages.brief: A bright display of painted eggshells, cascarones, rests together with colorful patterns. Around them, people celebrate in Mexico and the United States, smiling in a festive setting. The painted shells are the focus, showing how cascarones help people celebrate.

pages.text: Cascarones are fun to make. Poke a hole in an eggshell.
pages.brief: A close view of a person's hands holding a whole eggshell. A finger presses gently to make a hole in the shell. The person works carefully, starting the fun craft of making cascarones.

pages.text: Cascarones are fun to make. Take the egg out of the shell.
pages.brief: A person holds an eggshell with a small opening and carefully takes the egg out. The empty shell remains intact. This is part of making cascarones, showing the egg being removed from the shell and the shell kept for the craft.

pages.text: Cascarones are fun to make. Fill the egg with confetti.
pages.brief: A person fills an empty eggshell with colorful confetti. Hands guide the confetti into the small opening. The shell is being prepared as a cascaron, with bright pieces packed inside for the celebration craft.

pages.text: Cascarones are painted many ways. Cascarones make people laugh.
pages.brief: Several cascarones are painted in many different ways, with bright colors and patterns. People nearby laugh and smile, showing how cascarones make people laugh. The painted eggshells are the main focus in a cheerful scene.

pages.text: Some cascarones are painted with faces. Cascarones make people laugh.
pages.brief: Some cascarones are painted with faces. The eggshells show simple painted eyes, noses, and smiling mouths. People laugh as they look at the funny face designs, and the painted cascarones are shown close together in a cheerful group.

pages.text: Some cascarones are painted with animals. Cascarones make people laugh.
pages.brief: Some cascarones are painted with animals. The eggshells show small painted creatures, each with simple shapes and bright colors. People laugh while looking at the animal designs, and the painted cascarones are displayed together in a happy scene.

pages.text: Some cascarones are painted with fruits. Cascarones make people laugh.
pages.brief: Some cascarones are painted with fruits. The eggshells show small painted fruit shapes in bright colors. People laugh as they look at the fruit designs, and the painted cascarones are shown together in a cheerful display.

pages.text: People crack cascarones over their friends’ heads.
pages.brief: People crack cascarones over their friends' heads. One person gently breaks a painted eggshell above a friend's head, and confetti falls. The friends are together, taking part in the playful tradition that makes people laugh.

pages.text: People say cascarones bring good luck!
pages.brief: People say cascarones bring good luck. A group of friends holds painted eggshells and smiles, celebrating together. The cascarones are shown as a happy tradition, with people sharing the belief that they bring good luck.

books.title: The Bald Eagle
books.art_why: Bald eagles, U.S. coins, flags and public buildings exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: The bald eagle is a symbol of the United States.
pages.brief: A bald eagle stands in a natural outdoor setting, white head and dark brown body clearly visible. Its yellow beak and talons show, and its wings are folded. The eagle faces forward with a steady, alert look. Soft daylight falls on its feathers.

pages.text: The United States has many symbols. A symbol is something that stands for something else.
pages.brief: A simple outline of the United States fills the background while several different symbol shapes stand in a row in front. Each shape is plain and distinct, suggesting that many symbols can stand for a country. The scene is uncluttered and bright.

pages.text: The bald eagle is strong. It stands for the strength of the United States.
pages.brief: A bald eagle stands powerfully on a high rock, wings slightly open, chest forward. Its strong body and sharp beak show strength. The eagle is outdoors in clear daylight, with a wide sky behind. No other animals or people are in view.

pages.text: The bald eagle is beautiful. It stands for the beauty of the United States.
pages.brief: A bald eagle perches in soft daylight, its white head and dark feathers clean and bright. Its wings are folded neatly, and its yellow beak is clear. The eagle looks calm and striking in a natural outdoor setting, with a smooth, open background that keeps attention on its beauty.

pages.text: The bald eagle is free. It stands for the freedom of the United States.
pages.brief: A bald eagle spreads its wide wings and rises through open air, flying freely above a natural landscape. Its white head and tail stand out against the dark body. The sky is broad and clear, and the eagle’s movement looks easy and unblocked.

pages.text: The bald eagle is on money in the United States. It is on many coins.
pages.brief: A close view of a United States coin shows a bald eagle stamped on its face. Several other coins lie nearby, each with clear eagle designs. The coins rest on a plain surface in bright light, and the eagle image is easy to see.

pages.text: The bald eagle is on flags in the United States. It is on many state flags.
pages.brief: A flag with a bald eagle design flies from a pole outdoors. Nearby, another state flag also shows a bald eagle. The flags hang clearly in daylight against an open sky, with no people in view. The eagle emblems are visible on the cloth.

pages.text: The bald eagle is on public buildings in the United States. It is on many city halls.
pages.brief: A public building, a city hall, stands in daylight. Above its entrance, a bald eagle carving is set into the stone. The building has a clear front and steps, and the eagle is easy to see. No people are in view.

pages.text: The bald eagle is the national bird of the United States.
pages.brief: A bald eagle stands in a natural outdoor setting, white head and dark body clear. It is shown alone as the national bird of the United States, with a steady, proud posture. Soft daylight falls on its feathers, and the background is simple and open.

pages.text: The bald eagle is an important symbol of the United States.
pages.brief: A bald eagle perches in clear daylight, white head and dark brown body strong and distinct. It looks steadily forward as an important symbol of the United States. The natural outdoor background is simple, keeping the eagle as the main subject.

books.title: Gaggle, Herd, and Pod
books.art_why: All the subjects are real animals and people that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Animals are everywhere. Sometimes they gather in groups. Animal groups have different names.
pages.brief: Many different animals stand, walk and fly in a wide outdoor scene, some close together in small clusters and others apart, showing that animals live all around the world and often gather in groups of different kinds.

pages.text: A group of geese is a gaggle. A gaggle of geese stands together.
pages.brief: A group of geese, called a gaggle, stands close together on open ground, their long necks and bodies facing different ways as they stay in one loose cluster, showing how these birds gather as a group.

pages.text: A group of bats is a colony. A colony of bats may leave its cave all at once.
pages.brief: A colony of bats streams out of a dark cave opening all at once, many small winged bodies filling the air in a rushing cloud as they leave the cave together in one swift movement.

pages.text: A murder is a group of crows. This murder gathers at sunset.
pages.brief: A group of crows, called a murder, gathers at sunset, their dark shapes grouped closely together as the low sun lights the sky behind them at the end of the day, showing the birds coming together as one group.

pages.text: A group of whales is a pod. A pod of whales swims together.
pages.brief: A pod of whales swims together through the wide open ocean, several large whales moving in the same direction through blue water, their bodies rising near the surface as they travel as one steady group.

pages.text: A smack is a group of jellyfish. A smack travels on ocean waves.
pages.brief: A smack of jellyfish drifts and travels on ocean waves, many soft-bodied jellyfish moving together through the water near the surface, their bell-shaped bodies pulsing as they ride the moving water in a loose group.

pages.text: A group of zebras is a herd. Sometimes a herd races together.
pages.brief: A herd of zebras races together across wide open ground, striped bodies running side by side in a group, their black-and-white stripes blurring as they move, showing the animals moving together as one great herd.

pages.text: A pack is a group of wolves. A pack works together to hunt.
pages.brief: A pack of wolves moves and works together to hunt, several wolves spreading across the land in a coordinated group, their bodies low and alert as they move through the open country, showing how the group acts as one.

pages.text: A group of humans can be a family. A group of humans can be a neighborhood. What other groups do you know?
pages.brief: People are shown as a family group and as a neighborhood group, with adults and children standing together near one another in each scene, showing two different kinds of human groups that people belong to.

books.title: Changing Seasons
books.art_why: Seasons are real-world weather and plants that photographs can show clearly.

pages.text: I live where the weather changes during the year. It changes with each season. We have four seasons.
pages.brief: A child stands outdoors in the place where they live, with the sky and ground showing weather that changes through the year. Around the child, the scene suggests the four seasons arriving one after another.

pages.text: Then comes winter. Then comes fall. Then comes summer. We start with spring.
pages.brief: A child stands beside four outdoor views of the seasons, starting with spring and then showing winter, fall and summer in that order. Each view shows different weather and plants, and the child looks from one view to the next.

pages.text: It is spring and the snow melts. It gets warmer, and plants begin to grow. The days get longer, and the nights get shorter. I wear my jacket.
pages.brief: A child wears a jacket outdoors in spring. Melting snow lies on the ground, small plants begin to grow, and the warmer day is bright and long. The child looks at the melting snow and the new plants, with a short night behind the scene.

pages.text: I wear my shorts. The days are long, and the nights are short. It gets hot, and the plants grow bigger. It is summer.
pages.brief: A child wears shorts outdoors in summer. The day is hot and long, the night is short, and the plants around the child have grown bigger. Bright sunlight fills the outdoor scene, and the child stands among the large plants.

pages.text: It is fall. It gets cooler, and the plants stop growing. The days get shorter, and the nights get longer. I wear my sweater.
pages.brief: A child wears a sweater outdoors in fall. The air is cooler, the plants have stopped growing, and the day is shorter with a longer night. The child stands in the outdoor scene as the light fades.

pages.text: I wear my coat. The snow begins to fall, and the days are short. It is cold, and many plants die. It is winter.
pages.brief: A child wears a coat outdoors in winter. Snow begins to fall, the day is short, and the cold air surrounds the child. Many plants in the outdoor scene have died, and the child stands in the falling snow.

pages.text: The weather has changed with each season. It got warmer and warmer. The days got longer and longer. Then it got cooler and cooler. The days got shorter and shorter.
pages.brief: The child stands in the same outdoor place as the weather changes across the seasons. It grows warmer and warmer, the days grow longer and longer, then it grows cooler and cooler and the days grow shorter and shorter.

pages.text: The cycle will start all over. Next, I will see spring again.
pages.brief: The child stands outdoors in the place where the seasons changed, as the cycle is ready to start all over. The same outdoor setting waits for the next season, and the child looks ahead to seeing spring again.

books.title: How Do They Move?
books.art_why: Real animals and their movement can be photographed today.

pages.text: Animals, animals, how do they move? These animals move on land. They have strong legs for hopping and jumping. Can you name them?
pages.brief: A group of land animals with strong legs is shown hopping and jumping on land. Their bodies are lifted in mid-motion, with legs bent and stretched as they move. The scene focuses only on these animals and the ground beneath them.

pages.text: Can you name them? They have strong legs for running. These animals move on land. Animals, animals, how do they move?
pages.brief: Land animals with strong legs are shown running across the ground. Their legs are stretched in long strides, and their bodies lean forward as they move quickly. The picture shows only the running animals and the land they move on.

pages.text: Animals, animals, how do they move? These animals move on land. They have many legs for crawling. Can you name them?
pages.brief: Several animals with many legs are shown crawling on land. Their many legs are spread along their bodies as they move close to the ground. The scene shows only these crawling animals and the ground beneath them.

pages.text: Can you name them? They have two legs for walking and running. These animals move on land. Animals, animals, how do they move?
pages.brief: Animals with two legs are shown walking and running on land. Their two legs support them as they step and move forward, with bodies upright and balanced. The scene shows only these two-legged animals and the land beneath them.

pages.text: Animals, animals, how do they move? These animals move in the air. They have wings for flying. Can you name them?
pages.brief: Animals with wings are shown flying in the air. Their wings are spread wide as they lift and move above the ground. The picture shows only these flying animals and the open air around them.

pages.text: Can you name them? They have fins and flippers for swimming. These animals move in water. Animals, animals, how do they move?
pages.brief: Animals with fins and flippers are shown swimming in water. Their fins and flippers are stretched out as they move through the water. The scene shows only these swimming animals and the water around them.

pages.text: Animals, animals, how do they move? These animals move in the trees. They have long arms for swinging. Can you name them?
pages.brief: Animals with long arms are shown moving in the trees. Their long arms reach out and hold as their bodies swing from place to place among the branches. The scene shows only these swinging animals and the trees.

pages.text: Can you name them? no wings, and no fins. They have no legs, no arms, These animals move on land. Animals, animals, how do they move?
pages.brief: Animals with no legs, no arms, no wings, and no fins are shown moving on land. Their long bodies bend and slide along the ground as they move forward. The scene shows only these limbless animals and the land beneath them.

books.title: Needs and Wants
books.art_why: Real children, food, coats, bikes and homes exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: We all need things. We need food, water, and air. We need a home and clothing, too.
pages.brief: A wooden table holds a plate of bread and fruit, a clear jug and glass of water, and a folded shirt beside a small model house. An open window lets fresh air into the simple, sunlit room, with no people in it.

pages.text: We want things that are fun. We want things that make us happy. We all want things.
pages.brief: Three children play together on a sunny grass lawn, one kicking a red ball, another holding a toy kite high, all laughing with wide smiles. Bright sky and flowers behind them show the fun things they enjoy.

pages.text: Erin needs water to drink. She wants a glass of lemonade.
pages.brief: Erin, a young girl with braided hair, leans over the kitchen counter and drinks from a cup of water. Beside her sits a tall glass of yellow lemonade with ice and a lemon slice, waiting untouched.

pages.text: He wants pasta for dinner. Jacob needs food to eat.
pages.brief: Jacob, a boy of about seven, sits at a dinner table with a bowl of pasta in front of him, twirling noodles on his fork. A napkin and a glass of water sit nearby in the warm kitchen.

pages.text: Erin needs a warm coat for the winter. She wants a long red coat.
pages.brief: Erin stands in a snowy yard zipped into a thick warm winter coat, hat and mittens, snow falling around her. A long red coat hangs on a rack beside her, and she looks at it hopefully.

pages.text: He wants some wind to fly his kite. Jacob needs air to breathe.
pages.brief: Jacob stands in an open park holding the string of a kite that lifts high into a windy blue sky. His cheeks are pink, leaves blow past, and he breathes the fresh air with a happy grin.

pages.text: Erin needs to stay safe from the storm. She wants to go under her bed.
pages.brief: Rain lashes the windows of a house at night as Erin crouches under her bed with a blanket, staying safe and dry. Thunder flashes outside, and her toys sit quietly on the floor nearby.

pages.text: He wants a new bike. Jacob needs a way to get to school.
pages.brief: Jacob stands beside a shiny new bicycle on the sidewalk outside his house, one hand on the handlebars. Down the street a school building and a path to it are visible in the morning light.

pages.text: Erin needs to read a book for school. She wants to read a funny book.
pages.brief: Erin sits cross-legged on a couch with a stack of school books beside her, holding one open book with a funny picture and smiling at the page. A lamp glows and a backpack leans against the couch.

pages.text: Do you really need those things? What kinds of things do you want?
pages.brief: A child sits on a bedroom floor surrounded by a plate of food, a water bottle, a warm coat, a book and a toy, chin resting in one hand, thinking. Soft light fills the quiet room.

books.title: Glassblowing
books.art_why: Glassblowing is a real craft that exists today, so photos can show the people, tools, oven and glass clearly.

pages.text: I am a glassblower. Watch me make a beautiful glass bowl.
pages.brief: An adult glassblower stands facing the viewer in work clothes, one hand lifted as if to say watch. They are ready to make a beautiful glass bowl. The scene shows only the glassblower and the promise of the bowl to come.

pages.text: The oven that holds the glass is very, very hot. The hot glass is runny, like honey.
pages.brief: A very, very hot oven glows with heat. Inside it, hot glass looks runny like honey, soft and golden. The glassblower stands near the oven, watching the hot glass soften. The oven is large and bright.

pages.text: I dip my long pipe into the hot glass. I roll the pipe on the table to smooth and cool the glass.
pages.brief: The glassblower dips a long pipe into the hot glass. Then they roll the pipe on a table to smooth and cool the glass. The pipe is long, and the hot glass gathers at its end.

pages.text: I blow into the pipe. I blow a bubble in the gooey glass. I try not to blow too hard.
pages.brief: The glassblower puts the pipe to their mouth and blows into it. A bubble forms in the gooey glass. They blow gently, trying not to blow too hard. The glass bubble is round and soft.

pages.text: I add other colors to make the bowl even more beautiful.
pages.brief: The glassblower adds other colors to the glass. The colors mix into the bowl-to-be, making it even more beautiful. Their hands are careful as they add the bright colors. The glass is still soft and gooey.

pages.text: I dip my pipe into the oven again. The oven makes the colors flow.
pages.brief: The glassblower dips the pipe into the oven again. The hot oven makes the colors flow and blend. The glass glows as the colors move together. The glassblower watches the colors swirl. The oven is very hot.

pages.text: My tools help me to shape the glass.
pages.brief: The glassblower holds tools that help shape the glass. The tools are close at hand as they work the soft glass into shape. The glass is still warm and bendable. They use the tools carefully.

pages.text: I spin the glass as fast as I can. The bowl gets wider and wider.
pages.brief: The glassblower spins the glass as fast as they can. The bowl gets wider and wider as it turns. The spinning glass opens out into a bowl shape. The glassblower's hands and pipe move quickly.

pages.text: I break off the pipe. I heat the glass again to make it smooth.
pages.brief: The glassblower breaks the glass off the pipe. Then they heat the glass again to make it smooth. The glass is still hot and glowing. The pipe is set aside as the glass is heated.

pages.text: The glass cools slowly. My beautiful bowl is done.
pages.brief: The glass bowl cools slowly on its own. The beautiful bowl is done. The glassblower stands beside the finished bowl, which is smooth and clear. The work is complete. The bowl shines. The glassblower looks at the finished bowl.

books.title: Weird White House Pets
books.art_why: The book describes real historical White House pets and real places, so photographs fit.

pages.text: But some very odd pets have lived and horses. They have had dogs, cats, birds, Most presidents have had pets. Odd Pets at the White House, too.
pages.brief: The White House is shown with several ordinary presidential pets—dogs, cats, birds and a horse—gathered near the building, while the page introduces that most presidents have had pets and that some very odd pets have lived there too.

pages.text: Sheep lived at the White House. They kept the grass trimmed.
pages.brief: On the White House lawn, a small flock of sheep stands and grazes on the grass. The sheep are outdoors on the lawn, feeding and keeping the grass trimmed, as the page says they did at the White House.

pages.text: A president walked it on a leash. A raccoon lived at the White House.
pages.brief: A president walks a raccoon on a leash across the White House grounds. The raccoon is on the leash beside him, showing that a raccoon lived at the White House and that a president walked it outdoors.

pages.text: A snake lived at the White House. A president’s daughter took care of it.
pages.brief: Inside the White House, a president’s daughter takes care of a snake. She is shown near the snake, looking after it, as the page says a snake lived at the White House and the president’s daughter cared for it.

pages.text: One pulled a president’s Goats lived at the White House. grandchildren in a cart.
pages.brief: At the White House, goats are shown outdoors. One goat pulls a cart carrying a president’s grandchildren, with the children seated in the cart as it moves along, showing the goats that lived at the White House.

pages.text: A flying squirrel lived at the White House. A president let it climb on him.
pages.brief: A flying squirrel climbs on a president at the White House. The president lets the small squirrel climb over him, showing the flying squirrel that lived at the White House and the president who allowed it to climb on him.

pages.text: A president walked them in Bears lived at the White House. the garden.
pages.brief: A president walks bears in the White House garden. The bears are outdoors with the president on the garden path, showing that bears lived at the White House and that a president walked them there.

pages.text: An alligator lived at the White House. It lived in a bathtub.
pages.brief: Inside the White House, an alligator is shown in a bathtub. The alligator sits in the tub, as the page says an alligator lived at the White House and that its home was a bathtub.

pages.text: They went to live at a zoo. a hippo were gifts to presidents. Elephants, lions, a tiger, and Pets That Couldn’t Stay.
pages.brief: At a zoo, an elephant, a lion, a tiger and a hippo are shown in zoo enclosures. These animals were gifts to presidents but could not stay at the White House, so they went to live at the zoo.

books.title: In a Chinese Garden
books.art_why: The book shows a real, present-day Chinese garden with water, rocks, trees and a gate.

pages.text: In a Chinese Garden.
pages.brief: A peaceful Chinese garden fills a wide view, with traditional garden shapes and soft greenery all around under gentle daylight. The calm scene feels inviting and quiet, ready for a visitor to step inside soon.

pages.text: I’m visiting a Chinese garden. I enter a gate without doors.
pages.brief: A young child stands at the entrance of a Chinese garden and steps through a gate with no doors. The open gate leads into the garden, and the child moves forward into the quiet space.

pages.text: I see a lot of water. It looks as smooth as a mirror. I can see things in it. I’m glad for water to drink.
pages.brief: A young child looks at a large area of still water in the Chinese garden. The water is smooth like a mirror, and things can be seen in its surface. The child is glad for water to drink.

pages.text: I see a huge rock. The rock looks so strong. It will not move or fall down. I’m glad I’m strong now, too.
pages.brief: A young child stands beside a huge rock in the Chinese garden. The rock looks strong and firmly placed, and it will not move or fall down. The child stands tall and is glad to feel strong now, too.

pages.text: I see trees. They stand tall and give shade. I’m glad for trees to rest under on a sunny day.
pages.brief: A young child stands under tall trees in the Chinese garden. The trees give shade on a sunny day, and the child rests beneath them. The child is glad for the trees and their cool shade.

pages.text: The Chinese garden is beautiful and peaceful. I’ll remember it whenever I see water, rocks, and trees.
pages.brief: A young child looks back at the beautiful, peaceful Chinese garden. Water, a rock and tall trees are visible in the calm scene. The child will remember the garden whenever seeing water, rocks and trees again.

pages.text: gate tree water.
pages.brief: A Chinese garden gate, a tall tree and still water are shown together in a calm outdoor scene. The gate stands open, the tree rises beside the water, and the garden looks peaceful and simple.
